row.basis: righteous and wicked ways
row.note: The commentary says the requested road is recognized by its travelers; Psalm 1:6 says YHWH knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes, making the walkers and their endpoint distinguish the two paths.

row.basis: shepherd leads on righteous paths
row.note: The commentary reads the straight road as a lived route shaped by its company; Psalm 23:3 has the shepherd restore the speaker and lead him on paths of righteousness, so guidance is personal and ongoing.

row.basis: Abraham's household keeps YHWH's way
row.note: The commentary says the blessed path is practiced, not inherited automatically; Genesis 18:19 says Abraham is chosen so his household and descendants keep YHWH's way by doing righteousness and justice.

row.basis: choose life or death, blessing or curse
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the blessed from wrath-struck and straying groups without making status hereditary; Deuteronomy sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and urges a choice, tying destination to response.

row.basis: one bears one's own guilt
row.note: The commentary says the road belongs to those who walk it, not to a blessed person's descendants by birth; Ezekiel says neither son nor father bears the other's guilt, locating judgment in each person's own conduct.

row.basis: the wicked can turn and live
row.note: The commentary treats straying as a state from which a person may return; Ezekiel says a wicked person who turns from sin and keeps justice will live, making the path recoverable.

row.basis: the righteous can turn away
row.note: The commentary refuses to make the blessed road an inherited, permanent label; Ezekiel also says a formerly righteous person who turns to wrongdoing will die, so past standing does not replace present walking.

row.basis: God leads Israel through the wilderness
row.note: The commentary calls the requested road an everyday route with a guide and fellow travelers; Exodus depicts YHWH going before Israel in cloud and fire to lead them on their journey, grounding the image in a people led together.

row.basis: the whole wilderness way
row.note: The commentary treats guidance as a path actually walked and tested; Deuteronomy asks Israel to remember the whole way YHWH led them for forty years, adding that the road forms the travelers as it brings them onward.

row.basis: nations learn and walk God's paths
row.note: The commentary says the path is identified by the people who walk it; Isaiah has many peoples invite one another to learn God's ways and walk in his paths, turning guidance into a shared, imitable course.

row.basis: voice says which way to walk
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a guided route from wandering; Isaiah 30:21 pictures a voice behind the hearer directing, “This is the way; walk in it,” when the hearer turns right or left.

row.basis: wanderers led on a straight way
row.note: The commentary contrasts lost wandering with a road that reaches its destination; Psalm 107:7 says God led the wanderers on a straight way to an inhabited city, joining guidance to arrival and shelter.

row.basis: righteous path brightens
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the straight path from straying by how its travelers proceed; Proverbs 4:18 compares the righteous path to dawn light growing brighter, giving the good road a visible direction.

row.basis: wicked stumble in darkness
row.note: The commentary says straying is a journey without a clear way; Proverbs 4:19 says the wicked way is darkness and its travelers do not know what makes them stumble.

row.basis: holy highway for the redeemed
row.note: The commentary insists that a road is defined by its destination and travelers; Isaiah describes a highway called holy on which the redeemed walk, with the unclean excluded, making holiness a quality of the company and course.

row.basis: God leads the blind on an unknown road
row.note: The commentary's straying image includes not knowing where one goes; Isaiah promises to lead the blind by an unfamiliar way, turn darkness to light, and not forsake them, so lostness can be met by divine guidance.

row.basis: each sheep turns to its own way
row.note: The commentary contrasts a shared road with paths lost by following the wrong company; Isaiah says all have gone astray like sheep, each turning to his own way, giving the collective image of dispersed travelers a moral edge.

row.basis: seek the good old way
row.note: The commentary describes a route inherited through the footprints of earlier walkers; Jeremiah calls the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, while the verse records their refusal.

row.basis: prayer to be led on level ground
row.note: The commentary reads the ayah as a direct request for guidance into the path of God's favored people; the psalmist asks God to teach his will and have the good spirit lead him on level ground, making the route itself a prayer.

row.basis: lost sheep asks to be sought
row.note: The commentary keeps the lost traveler distinct from the guide and the destination; Psalm 119:176 calls the speaker a lost sheep and asks God to seek him, adding that straying need not be the final identity.

row.basis: Ruth chooses Naomi's people and God
row.note: The commentary says the road's companions are joined by faithful walking rather than automatic descent; Ruth, a foreign widow, binds herself to Naomi's people and God, showing chosen belonging through shared life.

row.basis: choice between following YHWH and Baal
row.note: The commentary separates two opposed paths with a renewed negation; Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between two opinions and tells them to follow whichever god is truly God, making divided allegiance a concrete fork in the road.

row.basis: confession of having left truth's way
row.note: The commentary contrasts a road that reaches its goal with straying into loss; the condemned in Wisdom 5 confess that they left the way of truth, missed righteousness's light, and traveled trackless paths, turning the image into a retrospective confession.

row.basis: narrow route between fire and deep water
row.note: The commentary explicitly treats the straight path as lived conduct rather than a hair-thin bridge; 4 Ezra pictures the desired city as an inheritance reached by one path between fire and deep water, a distinct Jewish afterlife image that contrasts with the daily road described here.

row.basis: Torah is not an inheritance
row.note: The commentary says descendants do not inherit the blessed path without walking it; Avot tells the learner to prepare for Torah because it is not an inheritance, making study and practice rather than ancestry the condition of belonging.

row.basis: Noah walks with God, Abraham before God
row.note: The commentary makes following earlier walkers the way into the path; Genesis Rabbah interprets “walked with God” of Noah as needing support, but “walk before me” of Abraham as strength, changing the parallel into two forms of guided walking.

row.basis: feet guided into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary asks for guidance into a road walked by people; Luke's song says the dawn from on high will guide our feet into the way of peace and shine on those in darkness, joining guided steps to rescue from lostness.

row.basis: followers walk in light, not darkness
row.note: The commentary contrasts the guided road with wandering; Jesus says the one who follows him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life, explicitly tying a person's path to whom they follow.

row.basis: sheep follow the shepherd's voice
row.note: The commentary says the path is known by its walkers and their guide; John depicts the shepherd going ahead and the sheep following because they know his voice, making guidance a relationship shared by a flock.

row.basis: narrow way leads to life
row.note: The commentary says the Qur'anic road is ordinary lived conduct, not a trial bridge; Matthew's narrow road leads to life and is found by few, a close two-path comparison that also preserves a different emphasis on entry and destination.

row.basis: blessed inherit the kingdom at judgment
row.note: The commentary names those receiving God's favor and sets them apart from the wrath-struck and straying; at judgment the Son of Man calls the sheep blessed by his Father and invites them to inherit the kingdom, linking blessing to an eschatological company.

row.basis: cursed sent away at judgment
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the blessed from those under wrath; Matthew has the King send the goats away as cursed, supplying a judgment scene with a sharply separated opposite company.

row.basis: Abraham's descent is no guarantee
row.note: The commentary says the path does not pass automatically from blessed ancestors to descendants; John warns his hearers not to rely on “We have Abraham as father,” since God can raise Abraham's children from stones, shifting status to repentance and fruit.

row.basis: Abraham's children do Abraham's works
row.note: The commentary says the blessed road belongs to those who walk as earlier figures walked; Jesus says Abraham's true children would do Abraham's works, making kinship a matter of imitation rather than ancestry alone.

row.basis: Abraham's children walk in his faith's footsteps
row.note: The commentary describes a road as the trace left by its earlier travelers; Paul identifies Abraham's family with those who walk in the footsteps of the faith Abraham had, an unusually close formulation of the path's companions.

row.basis: shepherd seeks the lost sheep
row.note: The commentary's last group can be anyone who loses the way, and its camel image is a separated animal; Jesus' shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek one lost sheep, showing that the straying traveler remains sought and valued.

row.basis: straying sheep return to their shepherd
row.note: The commentary holds straying and return together rather than treating the lost as a fixed people; Peter says his hearers were like sheep going astray but have returned to the shepherd and guardian of their souls.

row.basis: two ways, life and death
row.note: The commentary separates the guided road from straying and asks the reader to recognize their travelers; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death, then distinguishes them by concrete conduct.

row.basis: two ways of light and darkness
row.note: The commentary sets the blessed path against distinct forms of ruin; Barnabas introduces two ways, light and darkness, and says their governing powers and travelers differ, offering an early Christian ethical map alongside the Qur'anic prayer.

row.basis: God finds and guards Israel in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary's image of lostness includes a traveler without a known route; Deuteronomy says God found Israel in a desert waste, guarded him, and cared for him, supplying a scriptural scene of the lost being gathered into God's care.

row.basis: Hebrew no'am, pleasantness
row.note: The commentary labels anʿamta with Arabic root n-ʿ-m and develops softness, ease, and favor as nearby resonances; Hebrew no'am in Psalm 90:17 asks that the Lord's pleasant favor rest on his servants and establish their work, a cognate echo without equating the senses.

row.basis: disciples of Abraham and Balaam
row.note: The commentary identifies the road by the character of its travelers; Avot distinguishes Abraham's disciples from Balaam's by their eye, spirit, and soul, so following a patriarch is ethical imitation rather than mere descent.

row.basis: repentant can rise beyond the righteous
row.note: The commentary says a straying person may return to the guided path; Berakhot teaches that penitents stand where the completely righteous cannot, giving rabbinic weight to movement between the categories.

row.basis: outsiders join the patriarchs' table
row.note: The commentary says the path's company is not inherited by blood; Jesus says people will come from east and west, north and south to dine in God's kingdom, while others claiming place are excluded, unsettling inherited privilege.

row.basis: people of faith are Abraham's children
row.note: The commentary makes the way of the blessed a path that can be joined by walking it; Paul calls those of faith Abraham's children, extending kinship by allegiance rather than genealogy.

row.basis: followers are called the Way
row.note: The commentary says the road is recognized by the people who walk it; Acts describes the Damascus believers as belonging to “the Way,” showing a Christian community named by its shared route.

row.basis: YHWH's straight ways and walkers
row.note: The commentary says a road is recognized by its travelers; Hosea closes by saying YHWH's ways are right, the righteous walk in them, and rebels stumble, a particularly compact formulation of the ayah's contrast.

row.basis: God teaches sinners the way
row.note: The commentary frames the ayah as a plea for guidance to the road of God's favored people; Psalm 25:8 says the good and upright Lord therefore teaches sinners his way, pairing divine character with instruction for the errant.

row.basis: God's paths are covenant love and faithfulness
row.note: The commentary identifies the good road by its walkers and destination; Psalm 25:10 says all the Lord's paths are steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant, specifying what the path offers its companions.

row.basis: remember mercy in wrath
row.note: The commentary places the bestowed favor beside those under wrath; Habakkuk asks God to revive his work and, in wrath, remember mercy, a prayer that holds judgment and favor together.

row.basis: Moses intercedes against divine anger
row.note: The commentary notes that the same people may move from received favor to feared wrath; after the calf, Moses asks God to turn from fierce anger against Israel, making intercession a response to that transition.

row.basis: God relents after the intercession
row.note: The commentary leaves return open after wrath; following Moses' plea in the calf episode, this verse says the Lord relented from the threatened disaster, showing the people's condition can change.

row.basis: anger is brief, favor lasts a lifetime
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes those who receive favor and those under wrath; the psalm says God's anger lasts a moment while his favor lasts a lifetime, giving the contrast a temporal shape.

row.basis: Abraham blessed to become a blessing
row.note: The commentary names a people by God's act of favor; God tells Abraham he will bless him and make him a blessing, so bestowed favor turns its recipient into a source of good for others.

row.basis: a new generation does not know YHWH
row.note: The commentary says the favored generations do not pass the path automatically to their heirs; Judges says the generation after Joshua arose without knowing YHWH or his deeds, explaining how descendants can lose the inherited way.

row.basis: descendants warned against their fathers' path
row.note: The commentary says descendants must walk as the favored did rather than inherit their standing; Psalm 78:8 urges the next generation not to be like their stubborn, faithless fathers, making faithful transmission a learned response.

row.basis: forgetting the giver leads to ruin
row.note: The commentary says favor can be lost when its recipients change their conduct; Deuteronomy warns that forgetting YHWH and following other gods will lead to destruction, a concrete reversal from gift to judgment.

row.basis: return and obey after curse
row.note: The commentary allows people who have strayed to return to the guided path; Deuteronomy pictures exiles returning to YHWH and obeying him with heart and soul, after the preceding blessings and curses have come upon them.

row.basis: repentance can turn sins into merits
row.note: The commentary treats guidance and straying as states that can change; Yoma interprets repentance from love as making prior deliberate sins count as merits, extending the possibility of reversal beyond simple pardon.

row.basis: mercy shown on the road defines the neighbor
row.note: The commentary says the way is known by the people who walk it; after the wounded traveler is passed by a priest and Levite, Jesus identifies the neighbor as the one who showed mercy and commands the hearer to do likewise.

row.basis: the foreigner returns to give God glory
row.note: The commentary links favor received from God with joining the company of the righteous; after ten are healed, Jesus asks why only the foreigner returned to give glory to God, distinguishing gratitude and return from merely receiving a gift.

row.basis: Christ leaves footsteps for followers
row.note: The commentary describes the requested path as the trace left by earlier walkers; Peter says Christ suffered leaving an example so others might follow in his steps, making the guide's life a traversable pattern.

row.basis: straight paths made crooked
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the straight route from being led astray; Paul rebukes Elymas for trying to make the Lord's straight paths crooked, a concrete image of a person redirecting others from the way.

row.basis: leaving the straight way to follow Balaam
row.note: The commentary says the path can be lost by following earlier strayers; Peter says false teachers abandoned the straight way and went astray, following Balaam's path, linking a changed route to the company one imitates.

row.basis: make straight paths for the feet
row.note: The commentary emphasizes a road walked by actual feet and the form of walking; Hebrews commands readers to make straight paths for their feet so the lame limb may be healed rather than put out of joint.

row.basis: walk in good works prepared by God
row.note: The commentary holds divine favor and human walking together; Ephesians says people are God's workmanship, created for good works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in, joining gift to practiced conduct.

row.basis: darkness leaves a traveler unsure where he goes
row.note: The commentary describes straying as a journey whose direction and destination disappear; Jesus warns that one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, giving that lostness a precise image.

row.basis: claimants excluded while patriarchs feast
row.note: The commentary says the path is not guaranteed by descent from blessed ancestors; Jesus pictures some seeing Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets in God's kingdom while they themselves are thrown out, reversing inherited confidence.

row.basis: Jesus joins disciples on the road
row.note: The commentary describes the path as a shared walk whose travelers can guide one another; on the Emmaus road Jesus draws near and walks with two disciples, then interprets the scriptures to them, making companionship part of how the route is understood.

row.basis: wrath falls on those obeying unrighteousness
row.note: The commentary distinguishes wrath-struck people from active wanderers while allowing their conditions to meet; Paul says those who disobey truth and obey unrighteousness receive wrath, explicitly connecting a chosen course with judgment.

row.basis: walking, standing, sitting as a progression
row.note: The commentary identifies a person's path by the company and actions along it; Augustine reads Psalm 1's movement from walking in wicked counsel to standing in sin's way and sitting among scoffers as increasing entrenchment, sharpening the way's moral development.
